judgments.title: SHARIFAH SORAYYA BINTI SYED MAHMOOD JAMALULLAIL v SYED MUNIF ALWI BIN SYED MAHMOOD JAMALULLAIL

parties.label: PLAINTIF
names: SHARIFAH SORAYYA BINTI SYED MAHMOOD JAMALULLAIL

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: SYED MUNIF ALWI BIN SYED MAHMOOD JAMALULLAIL

judgments.catchwords: 1. Two Siblings and Three Estates. 2. The contesting parties, as the sole surviving members of their immediate family, are entangled in a protracted and bitter dispute over the estates left behind by their late parents and brother. 3. The Plaintiff and the Defendant had initially elected to regulate the distribution of the estates through a Deed of Settlement executed between them. One might have expected this to bring finality to the matter. Alas, the passage of time, some ten years or so, has done little to quell their discord. Despite having taken what appeared to be a significant step towards resolving their differences, disagreements continued to simmer. Grievances deepened, trust eroded, and the relationship between the siblings deteriorated further. Eventually, the Plaintiff commenced the present suit against the Defendant, to which the Defendant responded with a counterclaim of his own. 7. At its core, the principal question is whether the Deed of Settlement dated 21 December 2018 constitutes a valid and binding agreement between the parties or whether, for the reasons advanced by the Defendant, it is liable to be declared void ab initio or otherwise unenforceable. 8. If the Deed of Settlement is found to be valid and binding, the Court must then determine whether the Defendant acted in breach of its terms, whether he is estopped from challenging its validity after having accepted benefits under the settlement, and whether the Plaintiff is entitled to the reliefs claimed. 9. The Court must also consider the Defendant's contention that the validity of the Deed of Settlement cannot be determined without reference to the applicable principles of Syariah law, including whether the Deed complies with the relevant requirements of Islamic law and the extent, if any, to which the Power of Attorney dated 5 November 2011 bears upon the issues in dispute.

judgments.title: AMIRHAMZAH BIN KARIM v Mahani Catherine Binti Hijjas & ors
judgments.catchwords: This representative action under s 9(c) of the Societies Act 1966 concerned the alleged misappropriation of RM6 million belonging to Dewan Perniagaan Melayu Malaysia (DPMM) — a RM5 million PMO grant and RM1 million from Redberry Sdn Bhd — channelled into a related foundation's account rather than DPMM Pusat's MED-approved account. The High Court held that DPMM Pusat, DPMM Pulau Pinang, and the Foundation are separate legal entities, so the transfer breached Article 29.3 of DPMM's Constitution. The funds were found to be diverted without MED approval and misapplied on a single politically-tinged Langkawi programme, rejecting the defences of mandate, blanket approval, and private arrangement as abandoned, contradicted by contemporaneous evidence, or departures from the pleadings. Breaches of fiduciary duty were established, but claims of personal misappropriation, conspiracy to injure, and exemplary damages were dismissed. The defendants were held liable as constructive trustees, with an order for account and inquiry, tracing, and general damages. Societies Act 1966; representative action; breach of fiduciary duty; constructive trust; misapplication of funds; personal misappropriation; separate legal personality; conflict of interest; departure from pleadings; conspiracy by unlawful means; adverse inference; account and inquiry; tracing.
judgments.judge: YA Puan Arziah binti Mohamed Apandi

judgments.title: SIVACHANDRAN A/L S JAYARAJAH v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.

judgments.title: SA Coconut Enterprise v MOHD SAYUTI BIN SULAIMAN & ors
judgments.catchwords: Appeal from the Sessions Court – Principles on appellate intervention - Claim for goods sold and delivered – Sessions judge dismissed Plaintiff’s claim– Whether Plaintiff has legal capacity to sue – Plaintiff commenced suit in its business name and not in the name of proprietor – Plaintiff is a sole proprietorship business – Action ought to have been commenced in the proprietor’s name – Whether there is a contractual or business relationship between Plaintiff and Defendant - Burden is on Plaintiff under Sections 101 and 102 of the Evidence Act 1950 to prove its case – No Purchase Orders issued by Defendant to Plaintiff – No Delivery Orders issued by Plaintiff to Defendant – Incumbent upon Plaintiff to lead evidence to prove Defendant ordered and took delivery – Plaintiff failed to call witnesses from Port Authority or lorry drivers or transporter – No evidence that payments deposited into Plaintiff’s bank account were for Defendant – Plaintiff had contractual relationship with which business entity in respect of the coconuts sold and delivered – No receipt produced by Plaintiff – Payment vouchers become an important piece of document evidencing payments from a payee – Payments were from a different entity than the Defendant – Failure of Plaintiff to adduce evidence of the non-existence of MJ Transport invites an adverse inference to be made according to section 114(g) Evidence Act 1950 – Sessions judge had considered all documentary and oral evidence
